records.content: A medical worker checks a patient at an Ebola treatment center in Bunia, Democratic Republic of the Congo, on Oct. 18. Xinhua News Agency / via Getty Oct. 27, 2026, 9:23 AM UTC / Source : The Associated Press By The Associated Press The fast-moving Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has reached 10,000 confirmed cases, government data showed Tuesday, as health authorities race to slow the spread of the disease in multiple African countries. It is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history, and nearly half of the 10,060 confirmed to have the virus have died, according to data from Congo’s Ministry of Health. That also makes it the deadliest outbreak of the disease in the country’s history. The outbreak declared in May is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. Response teams are battling armed conflict, poor roads and violence from residents fueled by mistrust and misinformation. Those obstacles compound the challenge of persuading people to report symptoms and accept care in communities that have endured years of violence and repeated epidemics. Compared with the West Africa Ebola outbreak of 2014-16 — history’s largest and deadliest with more than 28,000 cases, including over 11,000 deaths — this has had at least three times the number of cases and number of deaths in the time since it was declared. It has spread farther across Africa than any previous Ebola outbreak, reaching three regions with cases recorded in Kenya and Nigeria as well. It has so far been recorded in five countries, including Uganda and France, both of which have no active cases at the moment. A recurring problem in the spread in Africa is what appears to be lax surveillance efforts, as most of the first cases were confirmed long after people started showing symptoms or after traveling. In Congo, the disease has spread to 66 health zones across eight provinces, from three zones when it was first declared in May. Responders have told The Associated Press that they’re seeing treatment centers in some of those health zones getting overwhelmed, with people still skeptical and violent toward them, and that health workers are regularly going on strike to protest delayed or unpaid wages. A medical worker patrols an Ebola treatment center in Bunia on Oct. 18. Xinhua News Agency via Getty “Some people still don’t seem to understand the seriousness of the situation even though they are directly exposed to the risk,” said Sephora Bgosi with the Ebola burial team in Ituri province, the epicenter. “Ebola disease is extremely dangerous and can be deadly,” said Bgosi. About 80% of recorded cases are still coming from outside monitored contacts, showing there are ongoing chains of transmission that health authorities are not aware of. At least 95% of recorded cases are supposed to be coming from known contacts for officials to say the outbreak has largely been brought under control, the Africa CDC has said. At least half of deaths recorded are among people who have not been admitted to treatment centers, a sign that people are still not reporting symptoms at all in many areas. In many zones, health workers are battling challenges ranging from basic needs such as adequate vehicles to complex ones like persuading families to release their relatives who are sick with the disease or who have died from it and need to be buried safely. Last week at the Nia Nia health zone in Ituri province, some Ebola responders, including surveillance and community engagement officers, went on strike over unpaid bonuses owed since late August, a common trend across many affected localities. More than five months since the outbreak was declared, health workers are still being attacked by angry villagers, including on Saturday when a nurse was killed and another health worker severely injured while responding to an Ebola alert in Bafwasende, Tshopo province. The outbreak has disrupted essential health services that are already underfunded and overstretched and has shifted attention away from other disease outbreaks the country is battling, such as cholera. More pregnant women are dying as they avoid hospitals over fear of infection and isolation, causing maternal mortality to double in some provinces soon after the outbreak was declared. It has also disrupted routine healthcare services such as childhood vaccinations, interrupted schooling for children where millions are already out of school, caused trauma and stigma for affected families and further stretched the livelihoods of many already struggling with hardship

RSS feeds → Contact → Sign in Editors' picks | Epidemics | Mass death Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak passes 10 000 confirmed cases in DRC ByRishav Kothari Tuesday, October 27, 2026 18:15 UTCTuesday, October 27, 2026 18:16 UTC Follow us on Google News The Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) reached 10 060 confirmed cases and 4 887 confirmed deaths as of October 25, 2026, according to the country’s public health institute. Its situation report, published on October 26, recorded cases across 66 health zones in eight provinces. Image credit: ECDC Health authorities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo recorded 10 060 confirmed Bundibugyo Ebola cases and 4 887 confirmed deaths through October 25, 2026. A government report, published on October 26, also showed contact monitoring below the response target, with data available from five provinces. The report recorded 96 newly notified cases and 46 deaths as of October 25, including 40 community deaths and six in treatment centers. It listed 2 684 recoveries and a cumulative case-fatality ratio of 48.6%. Distribution of cumulative confirmed cases of Bundibugyo virus disease in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, as of October 20, 2026. Credit: WHO Contact monitoring remained below the 95% response target. Across the five provinces submitting contact-follow-up data for October 25, teams saw 16 205 of 19 853 listed contacts during the preceding 24 hours, a rate of 81.6%. This was not a complete measure for every affected province. The government report said that attacks and threats against response teams, including the killing of a nurse, had prevented Bafwasende health zone in Tshopo from submitting data. The World Health Organization (WHO) described transmission as sustained and high-level in its October 23 assessment. Its data through October 20 showed that 50 of 66 affected health zones had reported at least one new case during the preceding 21 days; the other 16 had reported no recent cases. Number of confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, by date of notification, as of October 20, 2026. Credit: WHO Number of deaths among confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo by date of notification, as of October 20, 2026. Credit: WHO In Kenya, WHO reported nine confirmed cases and two deaths as of October 26. All nine belonged to one connected cluster, with no evidence of wider community transmission. Twenty contacts were released from quarantine after completing 21 days without symptoms, while 98 remained in quarantine. Nigeria confirmed its imported case in Abuja on October 20. The Nigeria Center for Disease Control and Prevention listed 53 contacts in its October 24 situation report, replacing the earlier count of 44. Number of confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease cases in Kenya, by date of notification, as of October 21, 2026. Credit: WHO Swiss authorities said the patient was evacuated from Nigeria to Geneva on October 26 and was in stable condition. Her husband was isolated in Zurich as a close contact. He was not reported as a second confirmed case. Investigations into the patient’s source of infection continued. WHO’s October 23 update listed cases in five countries since the outbreak was declared on May 15: the DRC, Uganda, France, Kenya and Nigeria. Map of parts of DRC affected by Ebola Bundibugyo Virus outbreak in 2026. Credit: ECDC No approved vaccine or specific treatment is available for Bundibugyo virus disease. On October 23, researchers in Bunia vaccinated the first participant in the TUMAINI Phase 2/3 trial, which evaluates candidate vaccines including Ervebo. Ervebo is licensed against a different Ebola virus; its use in the trial does not establish protection against Bundibugyo. WHO’s October 23 report still cited its August 14 risk assessment: very high in the DRC, high in countries sharing its land borders, and low for the rest of the African Region and globally. WHO said that assessment was being revised and continued to advise against general travel or trade restrictions. Bundibugyo virus spreads through direct contact with infected blood or other bodily fluids, or contaminated materials. Symptoms can appear two to 21 days after infection, and people do not transmit the disease before symptoms begin. Early supportive care can improve survival. WHO classifies the epidemic as the largest Ebola disease outbreak ever recorded in the DRC, irrespective of virus species. records.content: Home Animals Biology Environment Health & Medicine Tech Travel Space Natureworldnews.com Let's Connect Trending climate change Earth whales Bundibugyo Ebola Cases Near 10,000 as Congo Starts First Vaccine Trial and U.S. Adds a Travel Attestation By Lucas Caldwell Published: Oct 26 2026, 9:36 PM EDT Facebook Twitter Linkedin Comment Mail Glody MURHABAZI | AFP via Getty Images Confirmed cases in the Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak reached 9,847, with 4,761 confirmed deaths, as of Oct. 23, according to the CDC's situation summary. Nearly all are in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which reports 9,816 cases and 4,757 deaths, and nearly half of confirmed patients have died. Two new developments change the picture. On Oct. 23, WHO announced the outbreak's first vaccine clinical trial, launched in Bunia, the capital of hard-hit Ituri province. And CDC now lists confirmed cases in Kenya and Nigeria, while warning that starting after 11:59 p.m. Eastern on Nov. 3, international passengers flying to the U.S. must attest they have not been in Congo in the previous 21 days. The U.S. public risk has not changed — CDC says no U.S. cases are linked to the outbreak and the risk to Americans and travelers "remains low." The new rules matter most for people traveling to or through Central and East Africa, airline passengers and health workers. A Rare Virus With No Proven Vaccine Bundibugyo virus is one of several species that cause Ebola disease, and it has been seen only rarely. It was first identified in 2007 in western Uganda, and Congo had a smaller Bundibugyo outbreak in 2012, according to the UK Health Security Agency. UKHSA calls the current event the largest Bundibugyo outbreak recorded and the second-largest Ebola outbreak to date. That history is the core problem — the licensed Ebola vaccine, Ervebo, and approved antibody treatments target the Zaire species, which caused the 2014-2016 West Africa epidemic. Nobody yet knows how well they protect against Bundibugyo. The new trial, called Tumaini, is designed to find out. It uses ring vaccination, immunizing contacts of patients, and will include pregnant women and children 12 and older, Al Jazeera reported. Participants are first receiving Ervebo to test cross-protection. Two Bundibugyo-specific candidates, from the University of Oxford and Moderna, are expected to join soon with funding from CEPI. WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said the trial will show "whether any of the vaccine candidates designed for Bundibugyo virus work." Conflict and Cross-Border Spread The outbreak is concentrated in eastern Congo, where armed conflict, displacement and heavy trade traffic complicate response. As of Oct. 11, UKHSA counted cases in 65 health zones across seven provinces. Ituri had 6,695 cases with new cases declining, while transmission persisted in North Kivu, with 1,911 cases, and Haut-Uele, with 383. Nature World News previously reported on violence affecting responders, including a burned displacement camp near Bunia that held an Ebola transit center and strikes by unpaid health workers. Insecurity limits contact tracing, which means chains of infection can be missed. The virus has also traveled. Uganda recorded 20 cases before WHO and Africa CDC declared its outbreak over on Aug. 27. Kenya has nine confirmed cases and two deaths, according to CDC, after a traveler from Congo flew into Nairobi in early October. Nigeria has one confirmed case, the first in West Africa, and France had one case that has recovered. Each imported case shows how road and air travel can carry the virus across borders within days. U.S. Readiness and Travel Rules CDC's measures focus on stopping importation. Travelers who were in Congo within 21 days of a flight cannot board commercial flights to the U.S., and U.S. citizens and nationals coming from Congo must stay outside the country for 21 days first. Those who were in Uganda or South Sudan must enter through designated airports for enhanced screening. About 500 CDC staff are working on the response, including more than 120 deployed abroad. CDC also briefed U.S. clinical laboratories on the outbreak during its Oct. 19 Laboratory Outreach Communication System call, part of keeping hospital labs prepared to handle suspect specimens safely. CDC's formal risk assessment, last updated Sept. 8, rates the general U.S. risk as low and states that the "likelihood of infection is extremely low," though any case would have high impact. Travel guidance is tiered. CDC advises avoiding all travel to Ituri and North Kivu, reconsidering nonessential travel to Haut-Uele and Tshopo, and taking enhanced precautions elsewhere in Congo and in Uganda. Risks, Warning Signs and What Comes Next The people at greatest risk are health workers and family caregivers in affected areas, who handle body fluids, along with people attending unsafe burials. For U.S. residents, risk is concentrated among travelers returning from affected regions and the clinicians who see them. Anyone who develops fever, severe headache, muscle pain, vomiting, diarrhea, or unexplained bleeding within 21 days of being in an affected country should call a health care provider before arriving, so the facility can prepare. People without such travel history do not need to take special precautions. Key unknowns include how well Ervebo protects against Bundibugyo, how much transmission goes undetected in insecure areas, and how the Nigerian patient was infected. Trial results will take time, since efficacy depends on enough exposures among participants. Oct. 19, 2026: CDC briefs U.S. clinical labs on the outbreak. Oct. 6, 2026: Kenya reports its first case, a traveler from Congo. Aug. 27, 2026: WHO and Africa CDC declare Uganda's outbreak over. May 15, 2026: Congo and Uganda declare the outbreak. The bottom line: the outbreak is nearing 10,000 confirmed cases and has reached West Africa, but the first vaccine trial has begun in its epicenter. U.S. risk remains low, and travelers should watch for the Nov. 3 attestation requirement. Bundibugyo is rare, no vaccine is proven against it, and conflict in eastern Congo limits tracing and care. What is the new vaccine trial? The Tumaini trial in Bunia is testing Ervebo for cross-protection, with Bundibugyo-specific candidates expected to join. Which countries have reported cases? Importantly, the instances of single infected persons creating multiple cases have demonstrated the significant global risk and challenge posed by this Ebola outbreak. As many as 8 or more cases have occurred from contact with a single infected person during this outbreak. Such persons causing a large number of transmissions are often called "superspreaders". Ebola has escaped the main epidemic affected country of Democratic Republic Congo (DRC) in multiple instances, and cases have started occurring in Kenya as well as Nigeria, one of the most populous countries in Africa i . Previously, an infected person had traveled from DRC to Uganda, causing a small outbreak, but there have been no new cases reported in Uganda recently. A person that traveled recently from DRC to Kenya died, and infected at least 8 others, one of whom has also died, and at least 134 contacts were traced ii . Kenya has released some of the quarantined contacts. The case in Nigeria was a Swiss national and was evacuated to a Swiss hospital for treatment. Previously, medical personnel working with the Doctors Without Borders (MSF/DWB) have been evacuated to Europe for treatment. The course of the clinical trial suggests that the trial will continue into Phase IIB part upon completion of the Phase IIA part. The NV-387 Oral Gummies as a Treatment for Ebola Phase II Clinical Trial in DRC is divided into two parts. The first part, Phase IIA, is designed to evaluate dosing regimens based on the severity of the disease, and requires approximately 20 patients. Enrollment began on September, 23, 2026. The end point is 28-day survival, as with other Ebola clinical trials. As such, the Phase IIA part will be completed once the last enrolled person completes 28 days. A clinical trial to evaluate vaccines, called "Tumaini" (meaning "Hope" in Swahili) has started as of last week. Unmatched vaccines can cause rapid occurrence of escape mutants. Also, in vaccinated persons, later infection can even cause a more aggressive disease, a phenomenon called "Antibody-Dependent Enhancement" of disease, promoted by the inaccurate antibodies created in response to the vaccine. Vaccines in general can lead to escape mutants. Ebola virus is an RNA virus and thus very capable of generating escape mutants. Vaccines are not useful for a person after infection. Also, a vaccine requires about 2-3 weeks for antibody response to be generated, and therefore is minimally protective before 3 weeks. If a second dose of vaccine is needed, it complicates the situation further, because the first dose only creates partial immunity. Thus an effective treatment is essential for combating a spreading epidemic such as the current Ebola epidemic. Infusions such as of antibody cocktails or small chemical drugs are only useful, if effective, when patients can be hospitalized for the duration until recovery, and are costly to store, transport, and administer. records.content: Wellness 1st person inoculated in trial for Ebola vaccine to protect against strain behind DRC outbreak 1:17 AP Kenya confirms 1st imported Ebola case Dieudonne Dirole/AP Photo By Mary Kekatos October 27, 2026, 8:44 PM The first person has been inoculated in a clinical trial for a vaccine that could help protect against the viral strain behind the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), according to Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders). Bundibugyo ebolavirus (BDBV), a rare variant of Ebola, is behind the DRC outbreak that has led to more than 10,000 cases and nearly 5,000 deaths, the World Health Organization Regional Office for Africa posted Tuesday . There are no currently no vaccines or treatments available to treat Bundibugyo virus. The Tumaini clinical trial, as it's known, is evaluating the safety, efficacy and immunogenicity -- meaning the ability to generate an immune response -- of several vaccine candidates. A health worker collects a blood sample from a patient before administering a dose of the Tumaini vaccine against Ebola virus, in Ituri, Congo, Oct. 23, 2026. Dieudonne Dirole/AP Photo Related Articles What we know about the spread of Ebola amid growing outbreak in DRC The trial is being co-sponsored and co-led by the Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale in the DRC and the University of Antwerp's Global Health Institute in Belgium. Partners include the Congo Ministry of Health, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI), Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, the World Health Organization, and the Institute of Tropical Medicine in Antwerp. Participants are made up of people who at the time of enrollment were contacts within the previous 21 days of a patient who is a newly confirmed case of Bundibugyo virus disease, according to a summary of the clinical trial posted on the National Institutes of Health website. A healthcare worker in protective clothing is disinfected by a colleague inside a treatment center for Ebola patients in Beni, North Kivu province, eastern Congo, Sept. 26, 2026. Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/AP Photo On day 1 of the trial, participants are randomized to receive either a BDBV vaccine candidate or standard treatment, according to the clinical trial summary. On day 29, all participants receive the alternative intervention so that every participant is offered a candidate vaccine while allowing the comparison between groups to remain blinded. An independent data monitoring committee will review data accumulated during the trial while additional vaccine candidates are added to the evaluation and others are discontinued if they are shown to be ineffective. "The overall aim is to generate robust evidence to support the use of BDBV vaccines for outbreak response and future epidemic preparedness," the summary states. Related Articles Nigerian medical groups call for nationwide measures after 1st Ebola case MSF said Monday that the first vaccine candidate being studied is ERVEBO, which was developed and licensed to protect against the Zaire ebolavirus, which is the deadliest Ebola strain. At least two Bundibugyo-specific vaccine candidates being developed by Moderna and the University of Oxford in collaboration with the Serum Institute of India, and funded by CEPI, will be tested, according to MSF, which also said the Tumaini trial will notably include children. "Children are among those hardest hit by the Ebola outbreak in certain regions, yet they have historically been underrepresented in clinical research," said Valérie Briand, head of MSF's research division, Epicentre. "The inclusion of pregnant women and children aged 12 years and older, as well as children from one year of age for the ERVEBO vaccine, represents an important step toward generating evidence for populations that are often excluded from clinical trials." records.content: 27th Oct, 2026 POLITICS OIL & GAS BUSINESS ENVIRONMENT WOMEN YOUTH EDUCATION AFRICA ADVERT RATES Ebola outbreak: Africa, Europe push for faster Bundibugyo vaccine trials Mon, Oct 26, 2026 By editor 4 MIN READ Health AFRICAN and European regulators have called for faster clinical trials of potential vaccines against Bundibugyo virus, a strain of Ebola responsible for an ongoing outbreak in parts of Africa. They made the call in a joint position paper made available to the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) on Monday by the African Medicines Agency (AMA) and the European Medicines Agency’s (EMA) Emergency Task Force. The paper sets out the minimum requirements for starting clinical trials and recommends ways to accelerate vaccine development without compromising scientific standards or participant safety. It followed a scientific consultation jointly convened by AMA, EMA and the World Health Organisation (WHO) August, bringing together experts to discuss ways to advance potential vaccines against Bundibugyo virus disease. It said the public health emergency in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), along with reported cases in Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria, made timely vaccine development a priority. The paper said that vaccine candidates should progress through the different phases of clinical trials without unnecessary delays, while maintaining rigorous scientific evaluation and adequate safeguards for participants, including vulnerable groups. The development comes as Nigeria responds to an imported case of Bundibugyo virus disease confirmed in Abuja on Oct. 20, underscoring the importance of regional surveillance, preparedness and cooperation. According to the paper, early-stage vaccine trials should ideally be conducted in Africa to facilitate the transition to larger efficacy studies involving populations affected by the outbreak. It also recommended non-human challenge studies to establish whether vaccine candidates have a reasonable prospect of advancing to Phase 2 or Phase 3 clinical trials. The paper identified a single-dose vaccine as preferable because it could be easier to deploy rapidly during an outbreak. It proposed a Phase 3 platform trial involving people who had been in close contact with confirmed cases, using a ring-trial approach to assess whether vaccination prevented the disease. Under this approach, multiple vaccine candidates could potentially be evaluated within the same trial, allowing researchers to assess their effectiveness more efficiently. It said studies involving children and pregnant women should begin once sufficient initial safety data had been obtained from adults, given that Bundibugyo virus disease could also affect these groups. On regulatory requirements, the position paper said that product-specific repeat-dose toxicity studies might not be necessary before the first phase or second phase of trials for vaccines developed using well-characterised platforms. It listed such platforms to include messenger RNA (mRNA) and certain viral-vector technologies. It said that such decisions would depend on available preclinical and clinical safety evidence, including findings from other vaccines developed using the same platform technology. “Repeat-dose toxicity studies can be deferred or waived where evidence from multiple vaccine candidates using the same platform shows that different antigens does not adversely affect the overall safety profile. “Non-clinical and clinical safety data from vaccines developed using similar platforms against related pathogens can also support such decisions,” it said. The paper urged vaccine developers to engage early with AMA and relevant African national regulatory authorities for scientific and regulatory advice. It also called for coordinated clinical trial assessments to ensure that evidence generated met requirements for subsequent regulatory decisions. Meanwhile, a separate development on Oct. 23 saw the first participant vaccinated in the Tumaini clinical trials in the DRC to evaluate potential vaccines against Bundibugyo virus. The trial represents part of ongoing efforts to generate evidence on vaccine candidates against the virus, for which no vaccine has been specifically approved. The position paper, however, does not constitute vaccine approval. “Potential candidates must undergo the required scientific evaluation to establish their safety and effectiveness before they can be authorised for public use,” it said. It urged vaccine developers and regulators to work together to accelerate research while protecting trial participants and maintaining the integrity of the evidence required for regulatory decisions. Infectious Disease > Ebola Congo's Ebola Outbreak Tops 10,000 Cases as Authorities Race to Slow the Spread — It is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history by Associated Press October 27, 2026 • 4 min read Add MedPage Today on Google MedpageToday (AP Photo/Sebastien Kitsa Musayi) The fast-moving Ebola outbreak in Congo has reached 10,000 confirmed cases, government data showed Tuesday, as health authorities race to slow the spread of the disease in multiple African countries. It is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history and nearly half of the 10,060 confirmed to have the virus have died, according to data from Congo's Ministry of Health. That also makes it the deadliest outbreak of the disease in the country's history. The outbreak declared in May is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. Response teams are battling armed conflict, poor roads, and violence from residents fueled by mistrust and misinformation. Those obstacles compound the challenge of persuading people to report symptoms and accept care in communities that have endured years of violence and repeated epidemics. Compared to the West Africa Ebola outbreak of 2014-2016 -- history's largest and deadliest with more than 28,000 cases, including over 11,000 deaths -- this has had at least three times the number of cases and number of deaths in the time since it was declared. It has spread farther across Africa than any previous Ebola outbreak, reaching three regions with cases recorded in Kenya and Nigeria as well. It's so far been recorded in five countries including Uganda and France, both of which have no active cases at the moment. A recurring problem in the spread in Africa is what appears to be lax surveillance efforts as most of the first cases were confirmed long after people started showing symptoms or after traveling. African health ministers are to hold a virtual summit on Wednesday to strengthen the continent's collective response. "Ebola is crossing borders. Our response must move faster, with stronger coordination, greater solidarity, and decisive political leadership," Jean Kaseya, MD, head of Africa CDC, has said. At least 2,600 patients have recovered from the disease in Congo, bringing rare moments of joy to affected communities. A viral video this week showed health workers in full protective gear dancing as the last two patients were discharged from a treatment center in Mongbwalu, Ituri province. "The outbreak is far from over, but every life saved is worth celebrating," World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, PhD, said of the video. 80% of New Cases in Congo Are Outside of Monitored Contacts In Congo, the disease has spread to 66 health zones across eight provinces, from three zones when it was first declared in May. Responders have told the Associated Press that they're seeing treatment centers in some of those health zones getting overwhelmed, people still skeptical and violent toward them, and health workers are regularly going on strike to protest delayed or unpaid wages. "Some people still don't seem to understand the seriousness of the situation even though they are directly exposed to the risk," said Sephora Bgosi with the Ebola burial team in Ituri province, the epicenter. "Ebola disease is extremely dangerous and can be deadly," said Bgosi. About 80% of recorded cases are still coming from outside of monitored contacts, showing there are ongoing chains of transmission that health authorities are not aware of. At least 95% of recorded cases are supposed to be coming from known contacts for officials to say the outbreak has largely been brought under control, the Africa CDC has said. At least half of deaths recorded are among people who have not been admitted to treatment centers, a sign that people are still not reporting symptoms at all in many areas. In many zones, health workers are battling challenges ranging from basic needs such as adequate vehicles to complex ones like persuading families to release their relatives who are sick with the disease or who have died from it and need to be buried safely. Last week at the Nia-Nia health zone in Ituri province, some Ebola responders, including surveillance and community engagement officers, went on strike over unpaid bonuses owed since late August, a common trend across many affected localities. More than 5 months since the outbreak was declared, health workers are still being attacked by angry villagers, including on Saturday when a nurse was killed and another health worker severely injured while responding to an Ebola alert in Bafwasende, Tshopo province. Outbreak Is Impacting Congo's Healthcare Services The outbreak has disrupted essential health services that are already underfunded and overstretched and has shifted attention away from other disease outbreaks the country is battling, such as cholera. More pregnant women are dying as they avoid hospitals over fear of infection and isolation, causing maternal mortality to double in some provinces soon after the outbreak was declared. It has also disrupted routine healthcare services such as childhood vaccinations, interrupted schooling for children where millions are already out of school, caused trauma and stigma for affected families, and further stretched the livelihoods of many already struggling with hardship. Check Symptoms The Phase 2/3 trial, known as Tumaini, was launched in Bunia, the capital of the hardest-hit Ituri Province, said the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations, which is funding and supporting the study. Discover more Track Outbreaks Study Biology Check Symptoms The trial comes amid a worsening Ebola crisis that has claimed more than 4,600 lives in the DRC since May. Despite the scale of the outbreak, no vaccine has yet been approved specifically against the Bundibugyo virus, Xinhua News Agency reported. Tumaini, meaning "hope" in Swahili, aims to assess the safety, immune responses and effectiveness of several vaccine candidates, particularly among people who have been in contact with confirmed Ebola patients and face a high risk of infection. Check Symptoms The trial uses an adaptive platform design, allowing multiple vaccine candidates to be evaluated within a single study through a ring vaccination approach targeting contacts of confirmed cases. The first vaccine entering the trial is Ervebo, which is already licensed to prevent disease caused by the Zaire Ebola virus but has not been proven effective against the Bundibugyo virus. Two additional vaccines specifically developed against the Bundibugyo virus, one by Moderna and another by the University of Oxford in collaboration with the Serum Institute of India, are expected to join the trial "shortly." "The launch of the Tumaini trial marks a critical step towards establishing whether candidate vaccines can effectively protect people against the Bundibugyo virus," said Chikwe Ihekweazu, executive director of the World Health Organization's Health Emergencies Program. WHO Regional Director for Africa Mohamed Janabi also welcomed the launch Friday, saying the trial would generate crucial evidence on candidate vaccines while strengthening the response to the ongoing outbreak and preparedness for future epidemics. According to the latest figures released late Wednesday by the DRC's health authorities, the country had recorded 9,704 confirmed Ebola cases, including 4,687 deaths, as of October 20, with a case fatality rate of 48.3 per cent. The epidemic was declared in the DRC on May 15 and designated a public health emergency of international concern by the WHO two days later. The Africa CDC subsequently declared it a public health emergency of continental security. The current Ebola outbreak has become the largest and deadliest ever recorded in the DRC and the second-largest Ebola outbreak globally, after the 2014-2016 West Africa epidemic. records.content: DR Congo begins pivotal Ebola vaccine trial as outbreak kills nearly 4,700 First shots administered in Bunia as uncontrolled spread of Bundibugyo strain offers a grim window to evaluate Merck, Moderna and Oxford candidates A pivotal trial of vaccines against the strain of Ebola that is driving a deadly outbreak across parts of Africa has begun in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where the epidemic originated and the vast majority of cases and deaths have occurred. The first participant was vaccinated on Friday in Bunia, eastern DR Congo, with Merck & Co’s Ervebo shot, which has been approved to guard against a different Ebola species. An experimental alternative developed specifically against Bundibugyo by Moderna Inc and another by the University of Oxford and Serum Institute of India could also be tested in the study within weeks. “I’m pretty confident that we have the window because the outbreak is not being brought under control,” Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations Chief Executive Officer Richard Hatchett said in an interview. DR Congo recorded 9,704 confirmed cases and 4,687 deaths as of October 20, according to the World Health Organization, and is the largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded in the country, irrespective of virus species. Infections linked to the outbreak have also been detected beyond its borders. Hatchett said the outbreak has become deeply embedded across a wide area, making it unlikely that traditional control measures will suppress it before researchers can determine whether the vaccines work. Conducting the trial will still be difficult, with armed groups and decades of instability complicating efforts to enrol and follow participants. The WHO said only about 80 per cent of more than 30,000 contacts under follow-up in DR Congo were reached in the latest 24-hour period, below its 95 per cent target. Ervebo was developed to protect against Zaire Ebola, but animal studies suggest it may reduce Bundibugyo infections and significantly lower mortality, Hatchett said. Researchers will need at least several months to determine its efficacy, depending largely on how quickly the trial can enrol enough people exposed to confirmed cases. If successful, the purpose-built vaccines could be produced at scale. Serum manufactured more than 600,000 dose equivalents of the Oxford vaccine’s drug substance within nine days of receiving the material needed to begin production, Hatchett said. “We could quickly move to having millions of doses of that vaccine,” he said. That could allow health authorities to shift from vaccinating contacts around known cases to broader campaigns in heavily affected areas. Bundibugyo virus was first identified almost two decades ago, but limited resources were concentrated on more frequently occurring Ebola species, according to Hatchett. In a better-prepared world, vaccines against known threats would be developed in advance and held ready for outbreaks, he said. “We’re not there yet.”

Korea, DMZ James Comey Water motorcycle Flávio Bolsonaro Noah Wyle World News Oct. 27, 2026 / 4:42 AM Swiss woman with Ebola evacuated from Nigeria to Switzerland By Darryl Coote Oct. 27 (UPI) -- A Swiss national infected with Ebola and her husband have arrived in Switzerland after being medically evacuated from Nigeria, according to Swiss health officials. The woman and her husband, both Swiss nationals, arrived in Switzerland Monday, Switzerland's Federal Office of Public Health said in a statement, adding that the woman was being treated at Geneva University Hospital, while her husband was in isolation at Zurich University Hospital. "The HUG and the USZ are equipped to deal with such cases and can manage the individuals concerned while at the same time ensuring the safety both of staff and of all other patients," the public health office said. "This situation does not pose any risk to the population in Switzerland." The announcement of their arrival in Switzerland came hours after Nigerian Minister of Health and Social Welfare Muhammad Ali Pate announced their departure. "I confirm that, with my approval, earlier this morning, the index case for Nigeria's first imported Ebola virus disease departed Abuja for Switzerland," he said in a statement. The woman is Nigeria's first Ebola case since 2014. Health officials said she had arrived in the country from Uganda aboard an international flight. She developed symptoms on Oct. 7 and was admitted to a private hospital in the Nigerian capital of Abuja on Oct. 11. Pate said Monday that the woman was "clinically much improved, stable, conscious, communicating" and her clinical laboratory test results were approaching baseline. "This does not mean she is not still infectious, hence the strict protocols in place." Mohamed Janabi, the African regional director for the World Health Organization, said the couple were evacuated because both were Swiss citizens and the woman's conditions was clinically stable. "The Nigerian medical team successfully managed her through the acute phase of the illness and stabilized her condition," he said in a statement. "With the evacuation of the patient and her husband, Nigeria currently has no Ebola cases." Nigerian health officials will continue to monitor the 52 close contacts of the woman remaining in Nigeria, while Swiss authorities will monitor her husband, the 53rd identified contact. Janabi congratulated those involved in the woman's treatment and evacuation. "This is a remarkable achievement and a testament to what Africa can accomplish when we work together," he said. "This is a proud moment demonstrating African expertise, resilience and leadership in public health." Ebola update: The Ebola patient in Nigeria was medically evacuated to Switzerland earlier today, accompanied by her spouse, who remains without symptoms. The patient was stable and showing clinical improvement at the time of evacuation. Africa CDC congratulates Nigeria's emergency responders and health teams on their swift action and dedication to protecting communities. As response efforts continue, Africa CDC will support the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, NCDC and frontline teams with clinical guidance, infection prevention and control, decontamination of the health facility, and diplomatic and strategic advice. #AfricaResponds— Africa CDC (@AfricaCDC) October 26, 2026 The evacuation comes amid a multi-country Ebola outbreak caused by the rare and severe Bundibugyo virus. The earliest suspected case of the current outbreak was a healthcare worker in the Democratic Republic of Congo who developed symptoms in late April and subsequently died. The DRC declared an outbreak on May 15. Since then, there have been 9,995 confirmed cases and 4,845 deaths, the vast majority having occurred in the DRC, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Kenya has recorded nine confirmed cases and two deaths; Nigeria, the one case; and Uganda, 20 confirmed cases and 2 confirmed deaths along with one probable case and one probable death. France also confirmed a case, an intensive care doctors who was returning from a mission to the DRC in late June. The doctor fully recovered and was discharged from the hospital.
